title: why the glass breaks
hookLine: one stomp, a crunch, and everyone shouts mazel tov: why break something at a wedding?

cards: The end of the ceremony. The couple stands under a canopy. Someone sets a glass, wrapped in a cloth, on the floor.
One stomp, a crunch, and the whole room shouts mazel tov. Plenty of people have cheered for it without knowing why it happens. And there's more than one answer: families tell it different ways.

teach.h: THE CHUPPAH — OPEN ON EVERY SIDE.
teach.b: Start with the canopy. It's called a chuppah: four poles and a cloth, open on every side, like the roof of a home that's just beginning. Then the glass.
Its roots go back to rabbis in ancient Babylon who broke a precious cup at a wedding feast, on purpose, when the celebrating got out of hand.
Later teachers tied the custom to Jerusalem, and the Temple that stood there, destroyed nearly two thousand years ago. An old psalm promises to keep Jerusalem above even your highest joy.

So at the happiest moment, something breaks: a reminder that even on the best day, something in the world is still broken. Families add their own readings. Love is precious and breakable, so handle it with care.
A glass, once broken, stays broken; the promise is meant to be just as permanent.
In some old customs, the noise scared off bad luck. Traditionally the groom breaks it; at many weddings today, either partner does, or both together.
More than one meaning can be true at once, and a Jewish wedding is happy to hold them all. Then comes the shout, the words you met two days ago: mazel tov.

how: At the end of a Jewish wedding under the chuppah, a glass wrapped in cloth is broken underfoot, traditionally by the groom and at many weddings today by either partner or both, and the guests shout mazel tov.

games.q: the glass breaks, and for half a second the room is quiet. what happens next?
games.why: mazel tov! the crunch and the cheer come together: remember, then celebrate.

practice: Three breaths with the bell. First breath: the happiest moment you can remember. Second breath: someone or something missing from it.
Third breath: let the two sit side by side, without either one canceling the other.

wordCard.voice: The glass. Broken at the height of the joy, so the joy remembers. Fifth word.

orig.note: Hebrew: the breaking of the glass (kos, a cup or glass).

carryVoice: Your line: even in joy, remember. The crunch comes right before the cheering, never instead of it. That's day five.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 30b–31a (Mar son of Ravina and Rav Ashi break costly cups at wedding feasts)
Tosafot to Berakhot 31a (the custom of breaking a glass at weddings); Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chaim 560:2, with the Rema (remembering Jerusalem at a wedding)
Family explanations of the custom (fragility of love, an irreversible promise, warding off bad luck), as collected in the audience research (18Doors; Modern Tribe; Chabad.org)
